pos: n. (proper, queen mother of Judah; kin to the dew)
etymology: Hebrew Chamuwtal, probably father-in-law of the dew, or kinsman of dew. She was the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and her name is recorded three times — once for each of the two sons of Josiah who sat on David's throne and lost it.
biblical_def: The books of Kings judge every king of Judah by a fixed formula, and the formula includes his mother's name. Hamutal appears in it twice. “Jehoahaz was twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah” (2 Kings 23:31) — Jehoahaz was taken to Egypt and died there. Eleven years later, of her other son: “Zedekiah was twenty and one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah” (2 Kings 24:18), repeated word for word in Jeremiah 52:1. Zedekiah saw his sons slain before his eyes and was blinded and carried to Babylon. One woman of Libnah bore the last two kings of Judah of her line, and both reigns ended in captivity; her name is preserved in the formula that records it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, mother of Jehoahaz and of Zedekiah, kings of Judah.
webster_full: QUEEN MOTHER, n. A queen dowager who is also mother of the reigning sovereign; in Judah, an office of real influence.
LIBNAH, n. A city of Judah in the lowland, assigned to the priests; the birthplace of Hamutal.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy by force or the fate of war.
MOTHER, n. A female parent; especially, one of the human race; a woman who has borne a child.
scriptures: 2 Kings 23:31
Jehoahaz was twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
2 Kings 24:18
Zedekiah was twenty and one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
Jeremiah 52:1
Zedekiah was one and twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
2 Kings 24:19
And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.
corruption_summary: Motherhood is treated as private and historically insignificant, where the inspired formula for judging a king of Judah names his mother every time, before it names whether he did evil in the sight of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the name. The principle to recover is the weight Scripture gives to a woman most readers pass over. The royal formula in Kings is fixed: age at accession, length of reign, mother's name, and moral verdict. The mother is in the formula, every time, in the inspired record of the kingdom. That is not a courtesy. In Judah the queen mother held real standing, and the historian who wrote these summaries plainly considered that the household a king came out of belonged in the account of the king he became.

The sober side is that the naming is no guarantee. Hamutal is named with two sons, and both reigns ended in disaster — Jehoahaz dead in Egypt, Zedekiah blinded in Babylon with his sons slain before his eyes as the last thing he ever saw. Scripture never teaches that a godly or a notable household determines the outcome, and the same verses that record her name record that her sons did evil in the sight of the LORD according to all that their fathers had done. The record honours the mother and still holds the son responsible.

pos: n. (proper, elder daughter of Saul; Hebrew, increase)
etymology: Hebrew Merab, from rabah, to increase — increase, or multiplication. She was Saul's firstborn daughter, offered to David as a snare and then given to another man.
biblical_def: The family of Saul is set out plainly: “Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchishua: and the names of his two daughters were these; the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal” (1 Samuel 14:49). Then the offer, and the narrator's exposure of the motive behind it: “And Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him” (1 Samuel 18:17). Pious language — fight the LORD'S battles — concealing an attempt at murder by proxy. And then the promise was simply broken: “But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife” (1 Samuel 18:19). Merab is never recorded as speaking. She is offered, withdrawn and disposed of, and her five sons were afterwards hanged before the LORD in Gibeon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the elder daughter of Saul, promised to David and given to Adriel the Meholathite.
webster_full: BETROTH, v.t. To contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to promise or pledge one to be the future spouse of another.
PLEDGE, n. Something put in pawn; a warrant; a security; that which is deposited as security for the performance of an act.
SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals; anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble unexpectedly.
DOWRY, n. The money, goods or estate which a woman brings to her husband in marriage; or a gift given by the husband for the wife.
PRETEXT, n. Pretence; false appearance; ostensible reason or motive assigned or assumed as a color or cover.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 14:49
Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchishua: and the names of his two daughters were these; the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal:
1 Samuel 18:17

And Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him.
1 Samuel 18:19
But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife.
2 Samuel 21:8

But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:
corruption_summary: Marriage is now negotiated as a private arrangement between two adults, and Scripture's exposure of Merab's treatment goes unread — a father who used his daughter as bait and broke his word without a word from her.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the name. The live matter is the honesty of the narrative, which is easily missed because Merab is given no dialogue. Saul offers her with a spiritual exhortation attached — only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles — and the historian tells us in the next clause what Saul was actually thinking: let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him. Scripture refuses to let religious language cover the intent underneath it, and it exposes the king rather than the shepherd.

The second thing the passage establishes is that a daughter is not a counter to be played. Merab is promised and then handed to Adriel the Meholathite with no explanation, and David is left to face the shame of a broken betrothal. A father's authority over a household is real in Scripture and it is never absolute; it is held under God, for the good of those under it, and Saul's use of it here is set down as part of the record of a man the Spirit of the LORD had departed from. The record's sympathy is with the ones who had no voice in it.

pos: n. (proper, a wife of Elkanah; Hebrew, a pearl or coral)
etymology: Hebrew Peninnah, from peniynim, pearls or corals — the word Proverbs uses when it says the price of a virtuous woman is far above rubies. The irony of the name against the conduct is unlikely to be accidental.
biblical_def: The book of Samuel opens with a household divided by fruitfulness: “And he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children” (1 Samuel 1:2). At the yearly sacrifice the arithmetic of portions made the difference visible: “And when the time was that Elkanah offered, he gave to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and her daughters, portions” (1 Samuel 1:4), while to Hannah he gave a worthy portion, for he loved her, but the LORD had shut up her womb. The narrative then says that her adversary provoked her sore, to make her fret, and did so year by year when she went up to the house of the LORD. Peninnah is Scripture's portrait of a woman who had the thing another woman wanted and used it as a weapon — at the sanctuary, on the day of worship, annually. Out of Hannah's grief came a vow, and out of the vow came Samuel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the second wife of Elkanah, who had children and provoked the barren Hannah.
webster_full: ADVERSARY, n. An enemy or foe; one who has enmity at heart; an opponent.
PROVOKE, v.t. To call into action; to arouse; to excite; to make angry; to incense; to vex.
BARREN, a. Not producing young, or offspring; as, a barren woman; unfruitful.
POLYGAMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time; a practice recorded in Scripture and everywhere attended in it by strife.
PEARL, n. A hard, white, shining body, usually roundish, found in a testaceous fish; a thing of great value.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 1:2
And he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
1 Samuel 1:4
And when the time was that Elkanah offered, he gave to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and her daughters, portions:
1 Samuel 1:6
And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb.
1 Samuel 1:7
And as he did so year by year, when she went up to the house of the LORD, so she provoked her; therefore she wept, and did not eat.
corruption_summary: Scripture's record of polygamy is misread as its approval, when every polygamous household it describes — Elkanah's among them — is a scene of rivalry and grief.
corruption_paragraphs: It is sometimes urged that the Bible sanctions plural marriage because it records it without a formal prohibition in the narrative. The narratives themselves are the argument against it. Abraham's house, Jacob's house, Elkanah's house, David's house, Solomon's house — in every case Scripture shows contention, favouritism and grief, and here it gives the second wife the title her adversary. Our Lord settled the matter by going behind Moses to the creation: from the beginning it was not so, and a man shall cleave unto his wife, and they twain shall be one flesh.

The second observation concerns where and when the provoking happened. Peninnah provoked Hannah year by year, when she went up to the house of the LORD. The pilgrimage feast, the sacrifice and the sanctuary were the setting for the cruelty, and the occasion of worship was the occasion of the wound. Anyone who has watched a family gathering or a congregation used as cover for the same sort of thing knows the pattern is not ancient. What came out of it is the mercy of the chapter: Hannah went to the very God whose worship had been made a misery to her, poured out her soul, and was given a son she gave back.

pos: n. (proper, a wife of Lamech; Hebrew, shadow)
etymology: Hebrew Tsillah, from tsel, a shadow. She is one of the two wives of Lamech the Cainite, and her appearance marks the first polygamy recorded in Scripture and the first boast of vengeance.
biblical_def: The line of Cain reaches its climax in a man with two wives: “And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Genesis 4:19). This is the first departure from the one flesh of Genesis 2 that Scripture records, and it is recorded in the line of the murderer. Zillah's son is the father of metallurgy: “And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah” (Genesis 4:22). Then Lamech gathers both wives to hear a poem: “And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt” (Genesis 4:23), and he claims a vengeance seventy and sevenfold. Civilization's first arts — cattle, music, metal — and its first boast of unlimited revenge belong to the same household and the same chapter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the two wives of Lamech in the line of Cain, and the mother of Tubal-cain.
webster_full: POLYGAMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; retribution.
ARTIFICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind.
SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane.
BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture, often copper or bronze, wrought from the earliest times.
scriptures: Genesis 4:19
And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.
Genesis 4:22
And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah.
Genesis 4:23
And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. I
Genesis 4:24
If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.
corruption_summary: Technological advance is treated as moral advance, and Genesis 4 places the first metallurgy, the first music and the first polygamy in the same household as the first boast of unlimited revenge.
corruption_paragraphs: The story civilization tells about itself is that skill and progress travel together, so that a more capable society is a better one. Genesis 4 is arranged to deny it. In the line of Cain come tents and cattle, the harp and the organ, and every artificer in brass and iron — real goods, common grace, and Scripture does not sneer at any of them. In the same chapter, the same household and the same generation come the first plural marriage and Lamech's song, in which a man boasts of killing a young man for wounding him and claims a vengeance seventy and sevenfold. Capability increased; the heart did not change.

Our Lord answered that song directly. When Peter asked whether he should forgive seven times, Christ replied until seventy times seven — taking Lamech's number for vengeance and turning it into the measure of forgiveness. That is the gospel's reply to the line of Cain. Zillah and Adah were summoned to hear a boast of blood; the church is called to hear a word of pardon that runs to the same limit and beyond it, because the blood of Christ speaketh better things than that of Abel.

pos: n. (proper, a wife of Ashhur; Hebrew, a girl or maiden)
etymology: Hebrew Naarah, a girl, a maiden — the feminine of naar, a youth. She appears only in the genealogies of Chronicles, as one of the two wives of Ashur the father of Tekoa.
biblical_def: The whole of her record is two verses in the register of Judah: “And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:5). “And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:6). Nothing else is told — no deeds, no words, no death. She belongs to the great genealogies of 1 Chronicles 1 to 9, the nine chapters most readers skip, which the Chronicler compiled for a people just returned from exile who needed to know who they were and whose land it was. Tekoa is the town of the wise woman Joab employed and of the prophet Amos. In a book written to re-establish a nation's identity after captivity, a woman who did nothing the record relates except bear four sons is named twice and her sons are named after her.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the two wives of Ashur the father of Tekoa, in the genealogy of Judah.
webster_full: GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in order of succession.
REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings, for preserving and conveying knowledge.
TEKOA, n. A town of Judah south of Bethlehem; the home of the wise woman of 2 Samuel 14 and of the prophet Amos.
MAIDEN, n. An unmarried woman, or a young unmarried woman; a virgin.
POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 4:5
And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.
1 Chronicles 4:6
And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.
1 Chronicles 4:4
And Penuel the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. These are the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: The genealogies are treated as dead weight to be skipped, when they are the part of Scripture that insists ordinary people who did nothing famous are recorded by name in the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live habit is simply to skip. Nine chapters of names open 1 Chronicles, and most Bible readers pass over them with a clear conscience. But 2 Timothy 3:16 says all scripture is given by inspiration of God and is profitable, and that includes 1 Chronicles 4:6. The Chronicler wrote for a remnant just home from Babylon who had to prove their families, their priesthood and their claim to the land. Names were the documentary title of a restored people, and God saw fit to preserve them.

The quieter comfort is for everyone whose life will produce no narrative. Naarah has no recorded words and no recorded deeds. She had two things: a name and four sons, and both are in the Bible. The God who numbers the hairs of the head and notes the fall of a sparrow keeps registers, and the last of them is the book of life. Whether a person is remembered by history is a very different question from whether he is written down, and the genealogies exist in part to make that difference plain.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite who taught the law; Hebrew, majesty of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Howdiyah, majesty or splendour of Jehovah. He is one of the Levites named three times in Nehemiah, in the three scenes that together make up the reformation under Ezra: the teaching, the confession and the sealing of the covenant.
biblical_def: At the reading of the law, a body of named Levites did the work that made it effective: “Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place” (Nehemiah 8:7). Reading was not enough; the people had been in Babylon, and the sense had to be given. At the fast that followed, the same men led the confession: “Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever” (Nehemiah 9:5). And when the covenant was written and sealed, his name is in the list: “And their brethren, Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan” (Nehemiah 10:10). Teach, confess, subscribe — the same men in all three, and their names preserved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the Levites who caused the people to understand the law, led the confession, and sealed the covenant.
webster_full: LEVITE, n. One of the tribe or family of Levi; a descendant of Levi; particularly, one employed in the lower services of the temple.
EXPOUND, v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something to one's disadvantage; a public avowal of faith.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement; in Scripture, God's engagement with his people, and their sworn response.
CATECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
scriptures: Nehemiah 8:7

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.
Nehemiah 9:5

Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
Nehemiah 10:10
And their brethren, Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
Nehemiah 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Public reading of Scripture is often thought sufficient by itself, and exposition treated as an optional extra; Nehemiah 8 shows named Levites giving the sense so that the people understood the reading.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 8:8 states the method and it has never been improved on: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Four things in one verse — the text read, read distinctly, the sense given, and understanding produced. A generation raised in Babylon could hear Hebrew read and take nothing from it. The remedy was not to abandon the text for something more accessible but to station teachers among the people to open it. Preaching in the Reformed tradition is exactly this: not a lecture beside the Bible but the giving of the sense of the Bible.

The second thing is that it took a crowd of them, and Scripture names every one. Thirteen Levites are listed in verse 7, of whom Hodijah is one, and the same men reappear leading the confession and sealing the covenant. Teaching, repenting and committing were not divided among specialists; the men who explained the law were the men who stood up to bless the LORD and the men who put their names to the document. A church is in good health when those three things are found together in the same people, and their names are worth recording.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite of the restoration; also called Kelaiah)
etymology: Hebrew Qeliyta, dwarfed or maimed — a name of no dignity at all. Ezra records that he bore two names, and Scripture takes the trouble to tell the reader they belong to the same man.
biblical_def: He first appears in the painful list of those who had taken strange wives and put them away: “Also of the Levites; Jozabad, and Shimei, and Kelaiah, (the same is Kelita,) Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer” (Ezra 10:23). The parenthesis is the Holy Ghost's own footnote, joining the two names so no reader mistakes him for two men. He then appears among the Levites who “caused the people to understand the law” at the reading (Nehemiah 8:7), and finally among those who set their seal to the covenant: “And their brethren, Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan” (Nehemiah 10:10). The order of his three appearances is the point. A man named in the register of offenders is afterwards found teaching the law to the people and signing the covenant. Repentance in Ezra was not a private feeling; it was a public separation, and the man who made it was restored to public service.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Levite of the restoration, also called Kelaiah, who put away a strange wife and afterwards taught the law and sealed the covenant.
webster_full: REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow for any thing done or said; in theology, the pain, regret or affliction which a person feels on account of his past conduct, with a turning from it.
RESTORE, v.t. To bring back to a former state; to reinstate; to return to a good condition.
SEPARATE, v.t. To disunite; to divide; to sever; to part, in almost any manner.
SEAL, v.t. To fasten with a seal; to ratify; to confirm; to settle; to make fast.
REFORMATION, n. Change from worse to better; amendment of life, manners or of anything vicious or corrupt.
scriptures: Ezra 10:23
Also of the Levites; Jozabad, and Shimei, and Kelaiah, (the same is Kelita,) Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
Nehemiah 8:7

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.
Nehemiah 10:10
And their brethren, Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
Ezra 10:11
Now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives.
corruption_summary: Repentance is treated as a private change of feeling that need cost nothing publicly, and a man who has fallen is often either destroyed or restored without any visible turning; Ezra 10 required a costly separation and Nehemiah records the same man teaching afterwards.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 10 is a chapter the church finds hard, and it should. Ezra's charge was direct: Now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives. The sin in view was covenant-breaking with the surrounding nations, forbidden by name in the law, and the repentance demanded was visible and expensive. Whatever difficulties the chapter raises, it settles one thing: biblical repentance is not merely regret, and a sorrow that changes nothing a neighbour can see is not what Scripture means by the word.

The second half is the mercy, and it is easy to miss because it is scattered across two books. The Kelita of the offenders' list in Ezra 10 is the Kelita who teaches the law in Nehemiah 8 and seals the covenant in Nehemiah 10. A man whose fall is recorded by name in the word of God is recorded by name again among those instructing the people. Restoration in Scripture is neither cheap nor impossible. And the parenthesis that ties Kelaiah to Kelita is itself a kindness: God will not let the record be confused about who repented.
roots_summary: Hebrew Qeliyta (H7042), dwarfed or maimed; Qelayah (H7041), Kelaiah; badal (H914), to separate; yadah (H3034), to confess.
roots_lines: Hebrew Qeliyta (H7042) — Kelita; a name meaning dwarfed or maimed.
Hebrew Qelayah (H7041) — Kelaiah, his other name; the same is Kelita.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate; the action Ezra required.
Hebrew yadah (H3034) — to confess, to give thanks; make confession unto the LORD.
Hebrew chatham (H2856) — to seal; what he did to the covenant in Nehemiah 10.
usage: “Kelaiah, (the same is Kelita,)” — the Spirit's own footnote.
“Caused the people to understand the law” — the same man, restored.
“Make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure”.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite; Hebrew, the LORD has done wonderfully)
etymology: Hebrew Pelayah, from pala, to be wonderful or extraordinary — Jehovah has distinguished, or has done wonderfully. The root is the one used of God's marvellous works and of the name Wonderful in Isaiah 9.
biblical_def: One Pelaiah stands in the royal line after the exile, among the sons of Elioenai in the house of David: “And the sons of Elioenai were, Hodaiah, and Eliashib, and Pelaiah, and Akkub, and Johanan, and Dalaiah, and Anani, seven” (1 Chronicles 3:24) — the last verse of the Davidic genealogy in Chronicles, carrying the line forward in obscurity toward the Messiah. Another Pelaiah, or the same name borne by a Levite, is among those who “caused the people to understand the law” (Nehemiah 8:7) and among those who sealed the covenant (Nehemiah 10:10). The name is a confession: the LORD has done wonderfully. It was given in a household, carried through a captivity, and is found attached to men in the two places a restored Israel most needed them — in the line of David, and among those opening the Scriptures to the people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of a son of Elioenai in the line of David, and of a Levite who taught the law and sealed the covenant.
webster_full: WONDERFUL, a. Adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; a name given to the Messiah in Isaiah.
MARVELLOUS, a. Wonderful; strange; exciting wonder or some degree of surprise.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
NAME, n. That by which a person or thing is called; and among the Hebrews, frequently a confession or a memorial.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 3:24
And the sons of Elioenai were, Hodaiah, and Eliashib, and Pelaiah, and Akkub, and Johanan, and Dalaiah, and Anani, seven.
Nehemiah 8:7

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.
Nehemiah 10:10
And their brethren, Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
Isaiah 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
corruption_summary: Names are chosen now for sound and fashion, where Hebrew names were confessions carried in the mouth — and this one says the LORD has done wonderfully, in a generation that had seen the temple burned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a Hebrew name was a sentence. Pelaiah means the LORD has done wonderfully, from the same root as the marvellous works of the psalms and the Wonderful of Isaiah 9:6. Parents who gave it were putting a confession into a child's mouth for life, and every roll call in the household rehearsed it. Modern naming, governed by fashion and sound, has largely lost that, and with it a daily habit of confession built into ordinary speech.

What makes the name remarkable is when it was borne. 1 Chronicles 3:24 is the last verse of the Davidic genealogy, listing the descendants of a royal house that no longer had a throne, in a city whose temple had been burned and whose walls were rubble. In that setting a man is called the LORD has done wonderfully. And Nehemiah 8 shows the same name among the Levites opening the law to a people who wept when they heard it. Confession is not a claim that circumstances are good; it is a claim about God that outlives the circumstances, and the line it stood in ran on to Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew Pelayah (H6411), Jehovah has done wonderfully; pala (H6381), to be marvellous; Peleh (H6382), Wonderful; Elyowenay (H454), Elioenai.
roots_lines: Hebrew Pelayah (H6411) — Pelaiah; Jehovah has distinguished, or has done wonderfully.
Hebrew pala (H6381) — to be surpassing, marvellous, wonderful; the root of the name.
Hebrew Peleh (H6382) — a wonder; his name shall be called Wonderful, Isaiah 9:6.
Hebrew Elyowenay (H454) — Elioenai, toward Jehovah are mine eyes; his father.
Hebrew sheeriyth (H7611) — a remnant; the company these men belonged to.
usage: “The sons of Elioenai were... Pelaiah” — the last verse of David's line in Chronicles.
“Caused the people to understand the law” — the name among the teachers.
“His name shall be called Wonderful” — the root the name confesses.

pos: n. (proper, a brother of the Lord; a Greek form of Joseph)
etymology: Greek Ioses, a form of Joseph. The Authorized Version uses it of more than one man, chiefly of a brother of our Lord named in the two lists the townsmen of Nazareth recited when they took offence at him.
biblical_def: The men of Nazareth answered his teaching with his family tree: “Is not this the carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?” (Matthew 13:55). Mark records the same objection with the trade attached to Jesus himself: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended at him” (Mark 6:3). Joses is named second in both lists. At the cross and the tomb a Mary is identified by him: “And Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses beheld where he was laid” (Mark 15:47). The brethren of the Lord did not believe on him during his ministry, and after the resurrection they are found in the upper room with the disciples and with Mary his mother, continuing with one accord in prayer and supplication.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Greek form of Joseph, borne by a brother of the Lord named in Matthew 13 and Mark 6.
webster_full: BRETHREN, n. pl. Plural of brother; used in the solemn and scriptural style.
CARPENTER, n. An artificer who works in timber; a framer and builder of houses and of ships.
OFFEND, v.t. To displease; to make angry; to affront; in Scripture, to cause to stumble.
NAZARETH, n. A town of Galilee, the home of Joseph and Mary and the place of our Lord's upbringing.
UNBELIEF, n. Infidelity; disbelief of divine revelation; in Scripture, the sin of not receiving Christ.
scriptures: Matthew 13:55
Is not this the carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?
Mark 6:3
Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended at him.
Mark 15:47
And Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses beheld where he was laid.
John 7:5
For neither did his brethren believe in him.
corruption_summary: Familiarity is mistaken for knowledge: the men who knew our Lord's trade, mother and brothers by name concluded from that very knowledge that he could be nothing more, and were offended at him.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 6:3 is a warning aimed at everyone raised near the things of God. The townsmen were not ignorant; they were the best informed people in Galilee about Jesus of Nazareth. They knew his trade, his mother, his four brothers by name and his sisters by sight, and the conclusion they drew from all that information was and they were offended at him. Knowing a great deal about Christ, having grown up with the facts, is not the same as receiving him, and it can be the very thing that prevents it. He did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

The encouragement is what became of the brethren. John 7:5 states it without softening: For neither did his brethren believe in him. Joses is in that number. And after the resurrection, Acts 1:14 finds the apostles continuing in prayer “with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren”. James, named first in both lists, became a pillar of the Jerusalem church and wrote an epistle in which he calls himself a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ rather than his brother. Long unbelief in a family is not the end of the account; the risen Christ changed the minds of the men who grew up in his house.
roots_summary: Greek Ioses (G2500), Joses, a form of Joseph; adelphos (G80), a brother; tekton (G5045), a carpenter or builder; skandalizo (G4624), to cause to stumble.
roots_lines: Greek Ioses (G2500) — Joses; a Greek form of the Hebrew Joseph.
Greek adelphos (G80) — a brother; used of James, Joses, Simon and Judas.
Greek tekton (G5045) — a worker in wood or stone, a carpenter; our Lord's trade.
Greek skandalizo (G4624) — to put a stumbling block before; they were offended at him.
Greek homothumadon (G3661) — with one accord; the brethren in the upper room afterwards.
usage: “His brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?” — the town's objection.
“And they were offended at him” — the conclusion from knowing too much.
“Neither did his brethren believe in him” — and afterwards they did.

pos: n. (proper, a son of Simeon; Hebrew, right hand)
etymology: Hebrew Yamiyn, the right hand — the side of strength, of favour and of blessing. It is the same element that stands in Benjamin, son of the right hand. Three men bear it in Scripture, and the first heads a family of Simeon.
biblical_def: Jamin goes down into Egypt with Jacob's household: “And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman” (Genesis 46:10). At the second numbering in the wilderness his line has become a clan: “The sons of Simeon after their families: of Nemuel, the family of the Nemuelites: of Jamin, the family of the Jaminites: of Jachin, the family of the Jachinites” (Numbers 26:12). The Chronicler repeats the list for the returned exiles: “The sons of Simeon were, Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul” (1 Chronicles 4:24). Simeon's history is a lesson in itself — Jacob's dying words divided Simeon and Levi in Israel for their cruelty at Shechem, and Simeon's inheritance lay scattered inside Judah's. A third Jamin stands among the Levites who caused the people to understand the law (Nehemiah 8:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of a son of Simeon, head of the family of the Jaminites, and of a Levite in Nehemiah 8.
webster_full: RIGHT HAND, n. The hand on the right side; figuratively, the place of honor, strength and favor.
TRIBE, n. A family, race or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor.
FAMILY, n. The collective body of persons who live in one house and under one head; a race; a clan.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; in Scripture, the portion of a tribe in the land.
SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.
scriptures: Genesis 46:10
And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman.
Numbers 26:12
The sons of Simeon after their families: of Nemuel, the family of the Nemuelites: of Jamin, the family of the Jaminites: of Jachin, the family of the Jachinites:
1 Chronicles 4:24
The sons of Simeon were, Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul:
Genesis 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
corruption_summary: Consequences are expected to end with the man who earned them; Simeon's tribe carried the sentence of Jacob's dying words for centuries, and Scripture records the scattering without apology and without despair.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle in view is corporate consequence, which modern individualism finds hard. Jacob's last words over Simeon and Levi were a sentence on their cruelty at Shechem: Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel. It came to pass. Simeon's inheritance lay within the portion of Judah, and Simeon is the one tribe Moses omits from his blessing in Deuteronomy 33. Households and peoples really do carry the results of what their fathers did, and Scripture says so plainly.

It says something else just as plainly. The very same sentence fell on Levi, and Levi's scattering became the priesthood — the tribe with no inheritance but the LORD, dispersed through forty-eight cities to teach Jacob God's judgments. A curse of scattering turned into the means by which the whole nation was taught. God is not bound by the trajectory a family's sin sets. And the name Jamin itself, the right hand, is the side where the Son sits and where the sheep are gathered; a scattered tribe kept a name full of favour.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yamiyn (H3226), right hand; yamiyn (H3225), the right side; Shimown (H8095), Simeon, hearing; puwts (H6327), to scatter.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yamiyn (H3226) — Jamin; the right hand, the side of strength and favour.
Hebrew yamiyn (H3225) — the right hand; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Hebrew Binyamiyn (H1144) — Benjamin, son of the right hand; the same element.
Hebrew Shimown (H8095) — Simeon, hearing; the tribe Jamin's family belonged to.
Hebrew puwts (H6327) — to scatter, to disperse; Jacob's sentence on Simeon and Levi.
usage: “The sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin” — down into Egypt with Jacob.
“Of Jamin, the family of the Jaminites” — a man becomes a clan.
“I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” — and he did.
